Passages are summaries, not quotations: the linked source is the authority. Re-check each source and update reviewed_on in sources.json whenever a listed instrument is amended.

in-patent.title: Getting a patent in India
in-patent.caveat: Deadlines run from your own filing or priority date, and some differ for applications filed before 15 March 2024. Check each date against the cited Rules, or with a registered patent agent, before you act.

in-trade-mark.title: Registering a trade mark in India
in-trade-mark.caveat: Official fees and form versions change; check the current ones on IP India's trade mark pages before filing.

chunks.step_title: Keep the invention confidential and write it down
chunks.heading: Section 2(1)(l) — new invention
chunks.text: Do not publish, present, advertise or sell the invention before you file. A "new invention" under the Act is one not anticipated by publication in any document or by use, in India or elsewhere, before the filing date of the application with complete specification. Record what the formulation or process is, exactly what is new about it, and the experimental data showing its effect.

chunks.step_title: Search what is already known (prior art)
chunks.heading: 3.3 Examination; Annexure-I databases
chunks.text: The Patent Office tests novelty and inventive step of Ayush inventions against the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) and other databases, so search the same sources first: Indian patent records, international patent databases, and traditional-knowledge sources such as the TKDL and the Ayush Research Portal (ayushportal.nic.in), which the guidelines list in Annexure-I.

chunks.heading: Indian patent search
chunks.text: Search published and granted Indian patent applications free of charge on IP India's public search (InPASS) at iprsearch.ipindia.gov.in, by keyword, applicant, classification or application number.

chunks.heading: Access to the TKDL
chunks.text: The public TKDL website shows a representative database of Ayurvedic, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa formulations; access to the full database is available to patent offices only, under the TKDL Access Agreement. Treat a formulation documented in the classical texts as prior art even if you cannot see its TKDL record.

chunks.step_title: Check the three patentability tests and the exclusions
chunks.heading: Sections 2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(ac) and 3
chunks.text: An invention must be a new product or process, involve an inventive step (a technical advance or economic significance that is not obvious to a person skilled in the art) and be capable of industrial application. Section 3 excludes, among others: an invention that in effect is traditional knowledge or an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components (section 3(p)); a mere admixture giving only the aggregate of its components' properties (section 3(e)); and a new form or new use of a known substance without enhanced efficacy (section 3(d)).

chunks.heading: 3.4 Guiding principles 1–6
chunks.text: For Ayush inventions the Office applies these principles: an extract of a plant whose use is known is not novel, though a new process for obtaining it may be patentable; combining ingredients already known for the same disease is treated as obvious unless the specific combination or ratio shows an unexpected or synergistic effect; finding an optimum range by routine experimentation is not inventive; picking one ingredient out of a known formulation for the same use is not inventive; and new equipment or devices for known Ayush procedures may be patentable.

chunks.heading: Annexure-II — synergism
chunks.text: To show that a composition is more than a mere admixture under section 3(e), put experimental data in the specification proving that the combined effect of the ingredients is greater than the sum of their individual effects. The guidelines give worked illustrations of acceptable synergy data in Annexure-II.

chunks.step_title: Prepare the specification — provisional or complete
chunks.heading: Sections 9 and 10
chunks.text: The specification is filed on Form 2. You may file a provisional specification first to secure a filing date, but the complete specification must then be filed within twelve months of the filing date or the application is deemed abandoned (section 9(1)). The complete specification must fully describe the invention and the best method of performing it, end with claims, and disclose the source and geographical origin of any biological material used in the invention (section 10(4)(d)(ii)(D)).

chunks.heading: Section 6 as substituted by the 2023 amendment
section_path: Section 8 (amending section 6 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002)
chunks.text: If the invention is based on research or information on a biological resource accessed from India, or on traditional knowledge associated with it, the National Biodiversity Authority must be involved before the patent is granted: a person or entity covered by section 3(2) (broadly, foreign persons and foreign-controlled entities) needs the NBA's prior approval, and an Indian applicant covered by section 7 must register with the NBA; the Indian applicant then needs the NBA's prior approval at the time of commercialisation.

chunks.heading: Forms under the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2024
chunks.text: Use the NBA's current forms, filed online on the NBA ABS e-filing portal (absefiling.nbaindia.in): Form 7 for prior approval before grant of an intellectual property right (persons under section 3(2)); Form 8 for registration before grant (persons under section 7); Form 9 for prior approval at commercialisation after Form 8 registration. The old Form III no longer applies to these cases.

chunks.heading: Paras 17–18 — disclosure and NBA permission
chunks.text: Form 1 carries a declaration on whether the invention uses biological material from India, and the examiner raises an objection if the specification does not disclose the source and geographical origin of the biological material used.

chunks.heading: Forms 1, 2, 3, 5, 26 and 28
chunks.text: File Form 1 (application for grant), Form 2 (provisional or complete specification), Form 3 (statement and undertaking about corresponding applications abroad, under section 8), Form 5 (declaration as to inventorship), Form 26 (authorisation, if a patent agent files for you) and, to claim reduced fees, Form 28 (small entity, startup or educational institution). The application may be made by the true and first inventor, the inventor's assignee, or the legal representative of a deceased inventor (section 6).

chunks.heading: Where to file
chunks.text: File online through IP India's patent e-filing portal (ipronline.ipindia.gov.in). The appropriate office — Kolkata, Delhi, Mumbai or Chennai — is decided by where the first-named applicant resides, has a place of business or where the invention originated, or by the address for service in India for an applicant with none (Patents Rules, rule 4).

chunks.heading: Official fees
chunks.text: Official fees are set in the First Schedule to the Patents Rules, with lower fees for natural persons, startups, small entities and educational institutions; check the current amounts and download the forms on IP India's Forms and Official Fees page before filing.

chunks.heading: Sections 39 and 135
chunks.text: A person resident in India may not file for a patent outside India unless an Indian application for the same invention was filed at least six weeks earlier (with no secrecy direction), or the Controller has granted written permission, requested on Form 25 (section 39). An application in another convention country claiming priority from your Indian application must generally be made within twelve months, and the same twelve-month window applies in India for a convention application based on a foreign one (section 135).

chunks.heading: Rule 20(4) — national phase in India
chunks.text: An international (PCT) application designating India must enter the Indian national phase within thirty-one months from the priority date.

chunks.heading: Rules 24 and 24A
chunks.text: The application is published in the Official Journal of the Patent Office after eighteen months from the filing or priority date, whichever is earlier (rule 24). You can ask for early publication on Form 9 (rule 24A); it is then ordinarily published within one month of the request. After publication, anyone may file a pre-grant opposition (section 25(1)) until the patent is granted.

chunks.heading: Official Journal
chunks.text: Published applications and grants appear in the Official Journal of the Patent Office on IP India's journal portal, and the progress of your own application can be tracked on the application-status search at iprsearch.ipindia.gov.in.

chunks.heading: Rule 24B(1) as amended
chunks.text: Examination is not automatic. File a request for examination on Form 18 within thirty-one months from the priority date or filing date, whichever is earlier; applications filed before 15 March 2024 keep the earlier forty-eight-month period. If no request is made in time, the application is treated as withdrawn (section 11B(4)).

chunks.heading: Rule 24C — expedited examination
chunks.text: Expedited examination can be requested online on Form 18A where, among other grounds, the applicant is a startup or a small entity, a natural person applicant (or at least one of joint natural-person applicants) is female, the applicant is a Government department or Government-owned institution or company, or India was chosen as the International Searching or Preliminary Examining Authority for the corresponding PCT application.

chunks.heading: Rule 24B(3), (5) and (6); section 21
chunks.text: After examination the Controller issues a first statement of objections (the First Examination Report, FER). You must answer every objection and put the application in order for grant within six months from the date the FER is issued (rule 24B(5)); this can be extended once by three months on a request in Form 4 made before the six months expire (rule 24B(6)). An application not put in order within the time is deemed abandoned (section 21(1)).

chunks.heading: Sections 14 and 117A
chunks.text: If the examiner's report is adverse or requires amendment, the Controller must tell you the gist of the objections and, if you ask within the prescribed period, give you an opportunity to be heard before deciding (section 14). An appeal against a refusal lies to the High Court (section 117A).

chunks.heading: Chapter 09.05 — hearing
chunks.text: If your reply does not satisfy the requirements, or you contest an objection, the Controller offers a hearing and decides on the merits; hearings may be held by video-conference. File your written submissions and any supporting documents within fifteen days from the date of the hearing. After hearing you, the Controller may allow amendments and grant the patent, or refuse the application under section 15.

chunks.heading: Section 43
chunks.text: Once the application is found in order and not refused, the patent is granted with the seal of the Patent Office and the grant date is entered in the register. The Controller publishes the grant, after which the application, specification and related documents are open for public inspection.

chunks.heading: NBA approval or registration before grant
chunks.text: Where the invention is based on a biological resource accessed from India or associated traditional knowledge, the NBA approval (section 3(2) persons) or NBA registration (section 7 persons) must be in place before the grant.

chunks.heading: Section 25(1) and 25(2)
chunks.text: Before grant, any person may oppose a published application by representation to the Controller (section 25(1)). After grant, any person interested may give notice of opposition within one year from the date the grant is published (section 25(2)). Grounds include wrongful obtaining, prior publication, and that the invention is anticipated by traditional knowledge available within any local or indigenous community.

chunks.step_title: Pay renewal fees to keep the patent in force
chunks.heading: Rule 80; section 53
chunks.text: A patent lasts twenty years from the filing date (for a PCT application, from the international filing date) (section 53). Renewal fees fall due from the end of the second year and must be paid before each year expires (rule 80(1)); the time can be extended by up to six months on Form 4 (rule 80(1A)). Since the 2024 amendment, paying renewal fees electronically in advance for at least four years earns a ten per cent reduction. A patent whose renewal fee is not paid ceases to have effect.

chunks.heading: Rule 131(2) as substituted
chunks.text: Every patentee and licensee must file a statement of commercial working in India on Form 27 once for every period of three financial years, starting with the financial year after the year of grant, within six months after each period ends; the Controller may extend this by up to three months on a request in Form 4.

chunks.heading: What TKDL is
chunks.text: The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is India's database for protecting its traditional medicinal knowledge from misappropriation at international patent offices. It converts the classical texts of Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani, Sowa-Rigpa and Yoga into English, Japanese, French, German and Spanish, structured with the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification. The About TKDL page states that more than 4.54 lakh formulations and practices have been transcribed.

chunks.heading: Who can access TKDL
chunks.text: Access to the full TKDL database is available only to patent offices — sixteen of them, including the European Patent Office, the USPTO, the Japan Patent Office, the UK patent office and the Indian Patent Office — under the TKDL Access (non-disclosure) Agreement. Examiners may use it for search and examination only, and may not reveal its contents to third parties except as needed for citation. Pre-grant oppositions citing TKDL evidence are also filed at international patent offices.

chunks.heading: Conditions of use
chunks.text: Patent offices access TKDL at no cost. The Access Agreement does not permit TKDL content to be disclosed to third parties, except that a printout may be given to the patent applicant for the purpose of citation.

chunks.heading: What a TKDL record contains
chunks.text: TKDL is not itself the prior art: the classical books of the Indian systems of medicine are, and TKDL is the tool that makes them searchable. Each TKDL record gives the name of the drug, the origin of the knowledge, its constituents with the parts used and their quantities, the method of preparation and usage, and bibliographic details, with modern names for plants and diseases (for example Curcuma longa for turmeric).

chunks.heading: Status and limits of the database
section_path: Status and limits of the database
chunks.text: TKDL is a proprietary database of the Government of India. It is not exhaustive and does not affect rights relating to any traditional knowledge not listed in it, and it is not intended for medical or health advice.

chunks.heading: Books TKDL transcribes
chunks.text: TKDL transcribes 119 Ayurveda, 55 Unani, 91 Siddha, 1 Sowa-Rigpa and 15 Yoga texts — 281 in all, chosen on the advice of experts in each system. Its Source of Information page links the list of books for each system, with title, author and edition.

chunks.heading: The public representative database
chunks.text: Anyone can search TKDL's public representative database of about 1,250 formulations selected from classical texts of Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Sowa-Rigpa, by keyword, disease, IPC code, bibliography or title. Open it by choosing Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha or Sowa-Rigpa on the TKDL home page. It is a sample, not the full database.

chunks.heading: TKRC and patent classification
chunks.text: The Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) arranges Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha and Yoga knowledge in sections, classes and groups on the pattern of the International Patent Classification, and its codes are linked to IPC codes; TKDL states that TKRC led to about 200 subgroups under A61K 36/00 for medicinal plant preparations.

chunks.heading: Steps 01–02
chunks.text: Search existing trade marks for identical or similar marks, decide between a word mark and a logo mark, and identify the correct Nice class or classes for your goods; you can file a single-class or a multi-class application.

chunks.heading: Public search
chunks.text: Run the search on IP India's trade mark public search portal (tmsearch.ipindia.gov.in), by word, phonetic similarity or device, within the classes you intend to file in.

chunks.heading: Classification
section_path: Trade marks for goods and services (classification)
chunks.text: Trade marks are registered for specific goods or services grouped under the Nice Classification: classes 1–34 cover goods and classes 35–45 cover services. The registration protects the mark only for the goods and services listed, so describe them accurately.

chunks.heading: Class headings
chunks.text: Under the Nice Classification, medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations — including Ayurvedic medicines — fall in class 5, and cosmetics and non-medicated toiletries in class 3; foods and drinks fall in the food classes. Check the current edition's class headings and explanatory notes for your exact goods before filing.

chunks.heading: Steps 03–04
chunks.text: Confirm your applicant category (individual, startup, MSME or others), which decides the official fee, and prepare: applicant details, a clear representation of the mark, a description of the goods or services, a user affidavit with supporting documents if you claim prior use, and a power of attorney if an agent files for you.

chunks.heading: Steps 05–06
chunks.text: File a new application on Form TM-A (single-class or multi-class) through IP India's trade mark e-filing portal: log in, upload the documents and pay the prescribed fee.

chunks.heading: Steps 07–09
chunks.text: Track the application online. If the examination report raises objections, file a reply and attend the hearing if one is scheduled. The accepted application is published in the Trade Marks Journal, and third parties may oppose it within four months of publication.

chunks.heading: Validity and renewal of registration
chunks.text: A registered trade mark is valid for ten years from the date of application and can be renewed indefinitely for further periods of ten years by filing the renewal form with the fee. A mark that is not renewed may be removed from the register.

chunks.heading: What cannot be registered
chunks.text: Registration is refused for marks lacking distinctiveness, generic or descriptive terms, deceptive marks or marks likely to confuse the public, marks with prohibited or offensive matter, and marks identical or deceptively similar to existing marks. A brand made only of a classical formulation's name or an ingredient name therefore risks refusal as generic or descriptive; add a distinctive element.

chunks.heading: Filing an international application from India
chunks.text: To protect a brand abroad from India, file an international application under the Madrid Protocol through the Trade Marks Registry of IP India, based on your Indian trade mark application or registration, and designate the member countries where you want protection; WIPO records the international registration and each designated country examines the mark under its own law.

chunks.heading: Registration of copyright
section_path: Is it necessary to register a work to claim copyright?
chunks.text: Copyright arises automatically when an original work is created; registration with the Copyright Office is not mandatory but serves as evidence. Label artwork and packaging graphics are artistic works, product literature is a literary work, and computer programmes are literary works under section 2(o) of the Copyright Act, 1957.

chunks.heading: Who may apply; validity
chunks.text: A geographical indication is registered on an application in the prescribed form, addressed to the Registrar of Geographical Indications with the fee, by an association of persons or producers, or an organisation or authority representing the producers' interest — not by a single business for its own product. Registration is valid for ten years and can be renewed for further ten-year periods; individual producers of the goods can then register as authorised users.

chunks.heading: Where to file and search
chunks.text: GI applications are filed online on IP India's GI e-filing portal (online.ipindia.gov.in/eGir), and registered GIs and authorised users can be checked on the GI public search (search.ipindia.gov.in/GIRPublicSearch).

chunks.heading: Term and what can be registered
chunks.text: A registered design protects the new and original appearance applied to an article — for example the shape of a bottle, jar or pack — not how it works. Protection lasts ten years from the registration date (the filing or priority date), extendable once by five years to a maximum of fifteen; a design that is not new or original cannot be registered, so file before showing the design publicly.

chunks.heading: Where to file and search
chunks.text: Design applications are filed online on IP India's design e-filing portal (online.ipindia.gov.in/eDesign); search registered designs first on the design search at search.ipindia.gov.in/designsearch.

chunks.heading: Chapter I — the present position
chunks.text: India has no specific statute on trade secrets. Confidential formulations and know-how are protected through contract (non-disclosure and employment agreements), the common-law and equitable action for breach of confidence, and provisions of criminal law. The Law Commission's Report No. 289 (March 2024) recommended a dedicated law and proposed a draft bill; check whether Parliament has since enacted one.

chunks.heading: Section 7 as substituted — prior intimation
chunks.text: An Indian person or entity accessing a biological resource or associated knowledge for commercial utilisation must give prior intimation to the State Biodiversity Board. This does not apply to codified traditional knowledge, cultivated medicinal plants and their products, local people and communities including growers and cultivators, and vaids, hakims and registered AYUSH practitioners practising indigenous medicine for their livelihood; the cultivated-medicinal-plant exemption needs a certificate of origin from the Biodiversity Management Committee.

chunks.heading: Section 2(ea) — codified traditional knowledge
chunks.text: "Codified traditional knowledge" means knowledge derived from the authoritative books specified in the First Schedule to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 — the classical texts of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani.

chunks.heading: Applying to the NBA
chunks.text: Applications to the National Biodiversity Authority — for access approvals, intellectual-property approvals and registrations, and certificates of origin — are filed online on the NBA ABS e-filing portal (absefiling.nbaindia.in); fees are paid to the National Biodiversity Fund.

chunks.heading: Section 3(a) and 3(h); rule 158-B(I)
chunks.text: An Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug under section 3(a) is one manufactured exclusively to a formula described in the authoritative books listed in the First Schedule (a classical medicine). A patent or proprietary medicine under section 3(h) contains only ingredients mentioned in those books but is not itself a formulation in them, and is not given by parenteral route. Rule 158-B also lists as patent or proprietary medicines Balya/Poshak (health-promoting), Saundarya Prasadak (oral, skin, hair and body care) and Aushadh Ghana (plant extract) formulations.

chunks.heading: Rule 158-B(II) — safety and effectiveness
chunks.text: Rule 158-B sets the evidence for a manufacturing licence by category. A classical medicine made as per text for its textual indication needs no safety study and no proof of effectiveness; used for a new indication, proof of effectiveness is required. A patent or proprietary medicine with textual ingredients and textual rationale needs no safety study but needs published literature on its ingredients and a pilot study for effectiveness; if it contains any ingredient from Schedule E(1), safety and effectiveness evidence is required.

chunks.heading: Rules 152, 153 and 157
chunks.text: To manufacture Ayurvedic (including Siddha) or Unani drugs for sale, apply to the State Licensing Authority on Form 24-D; the licence is issued on Form 25-D. The manufacturing premises must meet the Good Manufacturing Practices in Schedule T, which the Licensing Authority verifies before issuing the GMP certificate.
topics: what do we need to manufacture

chunks.heading: Online licensing
chunks.text: Licence applications and other licence-related approvals for Ayurveda, Siddha, Sowa-Rigpa and Unani drugs are processed online through the Ministry of Ayush's e-Aushadhi portal; the portal's June 2026 guidelines make processing through it mandatory, and fresh ASU licence applications opened there from 28 April 2026.

chunks.heading: Rule 2(eb) — phytopharmaceutical drug
chunks.text: A phytopharmaceutical drug is a purified and standardised fraction of an extract of a medicinal plant or its part, with at least four defined bio-active or phyto-chemical compounds assessed qualitatively and quantitatively, for internal or external (not parenteral) use. It is regulated as a drug by the central drug regulator (CDSCO), not licensed on the authority of the classical texts; confirm the current approval pathway with CDSCO.

chunks.heading: Central drug regulator
chunks.text: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation is the national drug regulator under the Directorate General of Health Services. It administers the rules on new drugs, including phytopharmaceuticals, and on cosmetics; its website lists the current rules, guidance documents and online application systems. Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drug licences are issued by the State Licensing Authorities instead.

chunks.heading: Quality standards
chunks.text: Quality standards for Ayurvedic drugs and their raw materials are laid down in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, and the Ayurvedic Formulary of India describes the classical formulations; both are prepared by the Pharmacopoeia Commission for Indian Medicine & Homoeopathy under the Ministry of Ayush (pcimh.gov.in).

chunks.heading: Ayurveda Aahara
chunks.text: Foods made to Ayurvedic recipes and principles are regulated as food, not drugs, under the Food Safety and Standards (Ayurveda Aahara) Regulations, 2022, which require a licence or approval from FSSAI before such products are placed on the market and prescribe the Ayurveda Aahara logo. Read the regulation for the permitted recipes, claims and labelling rules that apply to your product.

chunks.heading: Where to apply
chunks.text: FSSAI licences and registrations for food businesses, including Ayurveda Aahara products, are applied for online on FSSAI's FoSCoS portal (foscos.fssai.gov.in).

chunks.heading: How the PCT works
chunks.text: The Patent Cooperation Treaty lets you file one international patent application that has effect in all PCT contracting states, followed by an international search report and written opinion. It does not grant an international patent: within the national-phase deadline (commonly 30 or 31 months from the priority date, depending on the country) you must enter each country where you want protection, and each national office decides on grant.

chunks.heading: Entering India
chunks.text: For India, the national phase must be entered within thirty-one months from the priority date (Indian Patents Rules, rule 20(4)(i)). Residents of India must also respect the foreign-filing rule in section 39 of the Patents Act before filing any application abroad.

chunks.heading: Right of priority
chunks.text: Under the Paris Convention, a first filing in one member country gives a right of priority for later filings in other member countries: twelve months for patents and utility models, and six months for industrial designs and trade marks.

chunks.heading: International prior-art search
chunks.text: WIPO's PATENTSCOPE database gives free access to published international (PCT) applications and to patent documents from many national and regional offices, and is the usual starting point for an international prior-art search.

chunks.heading: Madrid System
chunks.text: The Madrid System lets a trade mark owner protect a mark in many member countries with one international application and one set of fees, managed centrally through WIPO. The international application is based on a national application or registration and is filed through that office (for an Indian owner, the Trade Marks Registry of IP India), designating the countries where protection is wanted; each designated country examines the mark under its own law.

chunks.heading: Global Brand Database
chunks.text: Before designating countries, search WIPO's Global Brand Database, which combines trade mark records from international registrations and many national offices, for identical or similar marks.

chunks.heading: Nice Classification
chunks.text: The Nice Classification, administered by WIPO, groups goods into classes 1–34 and services into classes 35–45; it is used by India and most other offices. Medicinal and pharmaceutical preparations fall in class 5, and cosmetics and non-medicated toiletries in class 3 — check the current edition's class headings and explanatory notes for your exact goods.

chunks.heading: Hague System
chunks.text: The Hague System allows up to 100 industrial designs to be protected in its member territories through one international application filed with WIPO. Check WIPO's list of Hague members first: where your country of origin or target market is not a member, designs must be filed nationally.

chunks.heading: Disclosure requirement
chunks.text: The WIPO Treaty on Intellectual Property, Genetic Resources and Associated Traditional Knowledge, adopted in Geneva on 24 May 2024, requires patent applicants whose claimed invention is based on genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge to disclose the country of origin (or source) of the genetic resources and the Indigenous Peoples or local community providing the knowledge. It enters into force three months after fifteen eligible parties ratify or accede; check WIPO's treaty page for its current status and parties.

chunks.heading: WIPO work on traditional knowledge
chunks.text: WIPO's programme on genetic resources, traditional knowledge and traditional cultural expressions publishes the negotiating texts of its Intergovernmental Committee, practical guides on documenting traditional knowledge, and the GRATK Treaty; use it to understand how traditional knowledge is treated in international IP.

chunks.heading: Access and benefit-sharing
chunks.text: The Nagoya Protocol to the Convention on Biological Diversity requires that genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge be accessed with the prior informed consent of the providing country and on mutually agreed terms, with benefits shared fairly and equitably. Each party sets its own access rules — in India through the Biological Diversity Act and the National Biodiversity Authority.

chunks.heading: Finding a country's ABS requirements
chunks.text: The ABS Clearing-House lists each Nagoya Protocol party's national focal point, competent national authorities, legislative measures and internationally recognised certificates of compliance; check it for the access rules of every country whose genetic resources you use.
